Saratoga. In September and October of 1777, American forces commanded by Horatio Gates defeated British General John Burgoyne's army near Saratoga, New York. Burgoyne's strategy to divide the colonies by invading from Canada was ambitious but ultimately failed when his forces became surrounded and outnumbered. His supply lines were cut, he faced a growing American force, and he was unable to retreat safely. The climactic phase saw two major engagements: Freeman's Farm on September 19, and Bemis Heights on October 7. Burgoyne surrendered on October 17, 1777, with approximately 5,800 men—the first major American victory against a full British army in the field. The victory was as much about who was present as who fought. Marquis de Lafayette, a young French volunteer, fought alongside American forces and impressed Congress. Burgoyne's surrender triggered French diplomatic recognition of American independence and the formal Franco-American alliance in February of 1778, bringing French warships and soldiers into the war. This was the turning point that transformed French financial support into open alliance and global war.
